newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zairean rebels warned against building own state.
newsitem.headline: Zairean rebels warned against building own state.

text.p: After a string of military victories, Zairean rebels are coming under political pressure from the United States over fears they will set up a separate state in eastern Zaire.
In Uganda, the army said fighting raged in southwest Uganda on Thursday with Ugandan rebels based in eastern Zaire after at least 50 rebels were killed in battles on Wednesday.
Aid sources said a plane headed on Thursday to the northeast Zairean regional centre of Kisangani, which appeared quiet despite rebels saying it was surrounded by their forces.
The United States on Wednesday delivered a message to rebel leader Laurent Kabila, urging him to end murders and other human rights abuses against refugees returning to Rwanda.

"The message was essentially the following. The United States is deeply concerned about the allegations of political murders and human rights abuses in eastern Zaire by elements of the rebel alliance," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns told a briefing in Washington.
"The United States will not support in any way, shape, or form any effort by the rebel alliance to try to create any kind of artificial state in eastern Zaire," he said.

Burns also said Washington would not back any rebel move "to deny to the government of Zaire its responsibilities in maintaining the (eastern) international border with Rwanda and the other countries in Central Africa and East Africa."
But the rebels are already doing that -- since October they have seized control of a strip of Zairean territory 550 km (340 mile) long, running north-south parallel to the border with Rwanda.
Kabila says the rebels, originally known as the Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire, are determined to topple President Mobutu Sese Seko.
"The liberated area has no government yet," noted Kabila this week. "It is just part of the country free from Mobutu."
The rebellion has shown no signs of spreading to Kinshasa, 1,600 km (1,000 miles) west of the Rwandan border, and they admit the region in their hands needs to be governed.

Kabila has renamed the region, his rebel army and even the main river -- Eastern Zaire has become Democratic Congo, the rebel army has been renamed the Congolese Liberation Army, and the Zaire river flowing north has reverted to the name Congo.

Many Zaireans who have returned to their homes in rebel-held territory say they are happy to be no longer at the mercy of corrupt and ill-disciplined Zairean troops who for many years have been the most visible manifestation of Mobutu's rule.

The rebels have succeeded in blocking the deployment through their territory of a multinational force to help Rwandan refugees and Zaireans uprooted by fighting since October, arguing that its real aim is to restore Mobutu's grip on power.

In Uganda's capital Kampala, a Canadian spokesman said politicians would meet at the weekend, probably in Ottawa, to set a date for the multinational force to move aid to hundreds of thousands of refugees scattered by the fighting in Zaire.
Navy Lieutenant Charles Brown said the force so far had 340 soldiers in the region and 190 of these were helping set up a new headquarters at the Lugogo Centre, a trade and agricultural fair centre.

Kinshasa does not want airdrops of food for the refugees and it objects to the force using Uganda as its base. The rebels say that they will let in only a handful of ground troops and that the force is redundant because most refugees have gone home.
In Kasese in southwestern Uganda, an army spokesman said Ugandan troops were battling rebels of the mainly Moslem Allied Democratic Forces, which Uganda says is backed by Sudan.

He said at least 50 "invaders" were killed on Wednesday and five Ugandan soldiers and three civilians were wounded in the fighting on Ugandan territory, which followed a Ugandan army thrust into northeast Zaire from the Kasese region last week.
But civilians fleeing the area gave a civilian death toll of between three and five and said many others were wounded.
The spokesman said Ugandan troops heavily shelled Zaire on Tuesday and Wednesday and were likely to do so again on Thursday if the rebel attacks on Ugandan army positions persisted.

Fighting has raged in the southwest since last week when Ugandan troops crossed into Zaire with the blessing of President Yoweri Museveni, saying they were pursuing rebels. The Ugandan army says its troops only went three km (two miles) into Zaire.
Ugandan analysts say Kinshasa is not believed to have any link to the Ugandan rebels. The rebels pose no real threat to Museveni's rule and could soon be put down by the army.
Zaire accuses Uganda, Burundi and Rwanda of sending troops to fight alongside the Zairean rebels.
